lines.note: Mura is a village or settlement. This new entry is anticipated by the separate Mura catchword on the preceding page; the short body line is complete here.
The homographic Mura denotes unevenness or lack of uniform finish, rather than a village. The Portuguese begins a description of something made without equality and perfection.

runs.text: como couſa tinta, ou pintada bem em hũa par-

lines.note: Uneven dyeing or painting illustrates this second sense of Mura. The source preserves hũa and a visible par- division before the next row's te.
This completes the contrast between a well-finished part and a poorly finished one. The scan separates mal noutra; Qino mura- begins an example about removing unevenness from wood.
Qino mura- / uo nuqu is rendered as working and planing the wood well. The final pao is the historical Portuguese spelling, not an instruction to introduce a modern accent.
The object of planing is to leave no high or low spots. A further Mura- example then transfers this absence of unevenness to the quality of an art or accomplishment.
Mura-no nuqeta gueigia describes an art free of unevenness or defects. The scan has a word space before gueigia, correcting the OCR join; He begins the Portuguese statement that the art is perfect.

The continuation completes the description as free of imperfection and blemish. The word is imperfeição, with an f supported by its cross-stroke, not OCR imperſeição; mãcha keeps its nasal abbreviation.
Muracumo denotes scattered clouds of differing density. The headword's r is faint but its position is accounted for; nuuẽs and hũas preserve the printed nasal marks.
This completes eſ- / peßas and contrasts thick clouds with thin ones. The doubled-s ligature is retained rather than expanded or normalized to a different pair of s types.
Muradachi supplies principal forms for gathering or accumulating in groups. The Portuguese acumu- visibly continues as larſe on the following row.

runs.text: larſe ẽ varias partes, ou ẽ hũ lugar. ¶

lines.note: The gathering can occur in several places or in one place. Short nasal strokes are visible over both e forms and the u of hũ, so the OCR's è, e, and hu are corrected without expanding the abbreviations.
Nin- / juga muradatçu gives the example of people assembling in groups. The printed ma- at the right begins magotes on the following row.
The gathering is distributed, some groups here and others there. Cumo- begins a second example concerning clouds and retains its visible line-end division.
Cumo- / no muradatçu describes clouds massing together. The Japanese retains the historical genitive/subject particle spelling, and the Portuguese nuuẽs is not expanded.
This finishes the cloud example with the qualification that they gather in various ways. It is a genuine short continuation, not a missing or displaced headword.
The noun Muradachi names the gathering or accumulation described by the preceding verb. The Portuguese construction O ajuntarſe makes the nominal relation explicit.

runs.text: hum lugar, ou em varias partes. ¶

lines.note: The gathering may be in one place or dispersed over several. Ma- begins the example of a stand of pine trees, with a visible terminal division mark.
Ma- / tçuno muradachi is glossed as Pinheiral, a pine grove. The example applies the gathering sense to trees rather than animals or people.
Muragaraſu denotes a flock of crows. The source's long ſ in the final component is preserved, and the Portuguese coruos is not modernized.
Muragari gives principal forms for many birds or animals being together. The g in the headword is lightly impressed, but the word and following inflectional forms remain separable.
This completes the definition with animals together. The line is entirely Portuguese and remains a short indented continuation.
Muragariatçumari is a compound verb for assembling in numbers. The Portuguese Ajũtarſe retains its nasal abbreviation, while mui- continues into the next line.
Completing mui- / ta, the gloss encompasses many people, animals, and similar groups. Its breadth distinguishes this compound from an exclusively avian flocking verb.
Muraguiye describes snow melting unevenly. The printed principal forms and the deſ- division are retained, rather than replacing the Japanese spelling with modern forms.
This explains the unevenness: some portions of the snow have melted. The tilde stays on u in hũas, and the ampersand leads into the contrasting condition below.
Other portions remain unmelted. This short continuation is essential to the contrast in the Muraguiye definition.

runs.text: O derreterſe a neue em muitas par

lines.note: The noun Muraguiye names this patchy melting of snow. The line ends visibly in par without a secure hyphen; no division mark is supplied merely because partes continues below.
This completes par / tes and introduces Yuqino muragui- as an example of uneven snowmelt. Unlike the preceding Portuguese ending, the Japanese example has a visible terminal hyphen.
Yuqino muragui- / ye is translated as snow melted in this manner. The example repeats the noun while the Portuguese refers back to its patchy character.

runs.text: Murai muco. Qitaru coto naxi, ſaru coto

lines.note: Murai muco is explained by neither coming nor departing. The roman Japanese paraphrase continues across the line boundary after ſaru coto; its particles and spacing are retained as printed.

runs.text: O não vir, nem ſe tornar.

lines.note: Naxi completes the second negative phrase, followed by the translation of not coming or returning. The upright Bup. marks Buddhist usage and is kept outside the italic gloss, including its point.
Muramura is the reduplicated village term, glossed in the plural as villages or settlements. This contrasts with the unevenness and gathering senses of neighboring entries.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de vir, ou con-

lines.note: Muramurato is an adverb describing people arriving or assembling in successive groups. Adu. is italic apparatus, and con- visibly continues below.

runs.text: correr gente pouco a pouco de 20. em 20. ou

lines.note: The first illustrative group size is twenty at a time. Both printed 20. forms and the historical punctuation are retained rather than rewritten as prose numbers.
The next group size is fifty at a time: both leading digits have the same printed 5 form. The second OCR 30. is corrected to 50.; the Japanese example begins after italic Vt,.
Muramurato qiſoi quru describes people arriving or gathering in groups. The Portuguese rendering begins here and divides deſta after deſ-.
This completes deſ- / ta and specifies magòtes, groups or crowds. The grave accent on the o is visible and is not silently removed.
Muraſame is a sudden, forceful shower. The joined derepẽte and its nasal abbreviation are retained as printed, rather than regularized to modern spacing and spelling.
Muraſaqi is the purple color rendered here by Portuguese roxa. The roman headword and short italic color gloss form a complete single-line entry.

runs.text: Cor roxa quẽ dão ao fio com

lines.note: Muraſaqi ſuſogo names a purple coloring used for armor-lacing thread. The scan separates quẽ dão; the heavy oval mark above e may be a blotted diacritic or stray ink, so the aligned quẽ is retained with that nonblocking caveat rather than silently changed to expected que.
The thread is used to weave or lace the armor. The line completes the coloring explanation; armas here belongs to that historical armor context, not a separate headword.
Muraſuzume denotes a flock of sparrows. The source reads pardais in its Portuguese bird-name gloss.
Murataqe is equated with Taqe and translated as bamboo. Taqe follows the explanatory i, as a Japanese synonym, not a Japanese word embedded within Portuguese prose.
Muratori is a flock of birds. The Portuguese paßaros retains the printed doubled-s ligature, distinct from other visible s pairs elsewhere on the page.

runs.text: Atadura, ou liame de rota q̃

lines.note: Muraxiguedô denotes a rattan binding used on a shooting bow. The Portuguese reads Atadura, with u after d rather than OCR a; the headword has a circumflex, and q̃ remains abbreviated.
This specifies that the binding is on bows used for shooting. The line ends the column's body above the bottom rule and does not include the separate lower furniture.

runs.text: Chuuas do inuerno que vem derepẽ-

lines.note: Muraxigure denotes winter showers that arrive suddenly. The word derepẽ- is faint at the right edge; the aligned nasal abbreviation and terminal mark are retained for the continuation below.
The showers cease quickly, completing derepẽ- / te from the previous row. The doubled-s ligature in ceßão is preserved in the italic Portuguese gloss.
Mure supplies principal forms for animals or people assembling. The printed uru ending and Japanese headword remain roman, separate from the Portuguese definition.
The example Vchimurete fitoga quru describes people coming together in a crowd. Vir is entirely italic; the OCR's isolated roman i inside that Portuguese verb is corrected.
This completes the translation as people coming together in groups. The short line is the example's gloss and does not introduce another entry.

Mure j, iru, ita describes birds and animals remaining together. The scan really separates the final j-shaped i from Mure; the spacing and historical i/j allograph are retained, as is the visible pair of long ſ letters in paſſaros.
This completes ani- / maes and the description of being together. The line is a short indented continuation of Mure j, not a freestanding gloss.
This Muri is explained as Yumeno vchi, within a dream. It is a distinct homograph from the lack-of-reason entry below.
Sonhando restates the meaning as dreaming. Its italic type and final point complete the preceding dream-related entry.
The second Muri is Cotouari naxi, lacking reason or justification. Mu- begins the synonymous compound that continues on the next row.
Mu- / ri mutai is assigned the same sense by Idem. The source keeps the compound in two words rather than merging its Japanese components.
Murimeqi is a verb for making a noisy stamping or clattering sound. The historical Portuguese eſtropiada is retained, with the nature of the sound specified in the following line.

runs.text: cõ os pees como quẽ piſa taboas do telhado, &c.

lines.note: The comparison is to someone stepping on roof boards with their feet. Both cõ and quẽ have nasal strokes; the latter is not the OCR's grave-accented què, and pees retains its historical double vowel.

runs.text: Modo de ſoar, ou fazer estron-

lines.note: Muri muri is the corresponding sound-symbolic expression. Comparing the italic z with fazer in c2-l012 and c2-l032 shows that the apparent internal gap is the same letterform spacing, not a word boundary; the OCR faz er is joined, and estron- continues below.

runs.text: do com os pees, como quando hum anda ſobre

lines.note: The noise is again explained through the feet of a person walking above. The source prints hum in full here rather than the nasal abbreviation used elsewhere.
The roof boards complete the comparison. The continuation confirms the physical clattering sense, separate from the unrelated Muri entries for dreams and unreasonable behavior.

Murina and murino are alternative adjectival forms meaning unreasonable. Enlargement and comparison with deſarrezoada in c2-l038 show the same italic z followed by o, so the OCR's internal split is removed without modernizing the historical spelling.
Muriǒ is explained by Facari naxi, without measure, hence immense. The headword has a caron, and immẽſo retains the nasal abbreviation over e.
Muriǒ jinjin is glossed as infinite and immense. Both j-shaped consonants in jinjin descend below the baseline; they are not silently replaced by a more familiar-looking Japanese spelling.

The second element is mufen, boundless, not OCR muren. Its worn tall f retains the upper curl and cross-stroke position seen in the roman f of fitoga at c2-l004; the supplied NINJAL index independently agrees with this lexical reading. Idem gives the same infinite or immense sense.
Muriǒna is the adjective for something infinite or without number. The Portuguese definition explains the adjectival ending rather than adding a new unrelated meaning.
Muriǒni is the adverbial form, identified solely by Adu. No additional translation is invented for this genuinely short entry.
Muriǒ quǒdai combines immeasurability with vastness. Both caron-bearing Japanese forms are preserved, as is the nasal abbreviation in the Portuguese immẽſo.

runs.text: Forno onde fazem formento pera vinho

lines.note: Muro is described as the enclosure where the fermenting starter for rice wine is prepared. The source calls it a Forno and prints formento; those historical terms are not modernized.
De arroz specifies that the wine in the preceding definition is made from rice. The short continuation belongs to the brewing enclosure, not the following tree name.
A second Muro is identified simply as a tree name by Qinona and the Portuguese gloss. The page does not supply enough botanical detail to add a species identification to the transcription.
Mu rui is equated with Taguynaxi, having no equal. Both occurrences of Mu rui retain the printed internal space; the second begins an example continuing below.

runs.text: Couſa que não tem igual nem com-

lines.note: Mu rui / na coto is a thing without equal or comparison. The Portuguese com- is visibly divided before paração on the next row.
This completes com- / paração, finishing the example's explanation. The cedilla and nasal mark are retained as printed.
Muſa is paraphrased as Naſucoto naxi, doing nothing. The definition begins with not acting or being idle; the source's joined Naſucoto is not resegmented.
The gloss completes the inactivity sense, followed by Muſato xite iru. Estar ſem begins the example's translation, with the Japanese phrase remaining roman.
Fazer nada finishes the statement of being without anything to do. It is the completion of the preceding Portuguese phrase, not a separate imperative.
Muſabori denotes craving or strongly desiring something. Its printed principal forms u, otta are retained rather than rewritten as modern full conjugations.

runs.text: muito, ou procurar algũa couſa deſordenada

lines.note: The sense extends to seeking something in a disordered or excessive way. Deſordenada continues without a visible hyphen; the tilde in algũa is not expanded.
Completing deſordenada / mente, the entry gives Zaiuo muſaboru, coveting wealth. The example is roman between the two italic Portuguese passages.
The translation explains both strong desire for riches and pursuing them by bad means. Procuralas is printed joined and remains so; ruins qualifies the next row's meyos.
Meyos completes the phrase about bad means. Its historical y is retained, and the short line is not mistaken for a separate lexical item.
Muſacuſana describes an unreasonable or disorderly person or thing. Peſſoa has a visible pair of long ſ letters, which is retained instead of replacing it with the distinct ß sort found elsewhere.
The example describes encountering an unreasonable horseman. The printed yuqiyǒta, including its caron, is retained, and italic Vt, introduces the otherwise roman Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Encontrei com hum caualeiro de ſarre-

lines.note: Cura. appears as an upright source label between the example and its translation and is not expanded. The scan separates Encontrei com; the source's loose de ſarre- spelling and physical division are retained in the horseman description.
This completes de ſarre- / zoado, then gives an example of saying or doing unreasonable things. The alternatives yǔ and next-line ſuru are linked by the roman l,.
Completing the alternative Japanese verb, the gloss reads Dizer, ou fazer, to say or do. The a in fazer corrects OCR fuzer, while the terminal deſarrezoa- division remains visible.
This finishes deſarrezoa- / das and adds the idea of being outside the proper course. The phrase is part of the dictionary's explanation of unreasonable conduct.
Muſacuſani is the corresponding adverb, with only Aduer. supplied as its grammatical label. No unprinted definition is added to this short entry.
Muſai is equated with Saicacu naxi, lacking resourcefulness or practical ability. The Portuguese begins a description of being without prudence or skill.
Muſaino mi applies that lack of ability to oneself. The scan has u in Muſaino, not OCR n, and a real space in Eu igno-; the Portuguese self-description continues on the next line.
This completes igno- / rante and describes the speaker as without prudence. The line ends the body; the lower Muſai. is separate catchword furniture, not an additional entry on this page.
